result.summary: Mercury leads Laius' ghost up from the underworld to Thebes, where, disguised as Tiresias, Laius stirs Eteocles against Polynices. Polynices and Tydeus are accepted as sons-in-law by Adrastus, and Argia's cursed necklace is explained. Tydeus goes to Thebes as envoy, is rebuffed by Eteocles, and kills a fifty-man ambush before dedicating the spoils to Pallas.

scenes.title: Mercury leads Laius' ghost upward
scenes.summary: Mercury guides Laius' shade through the underworld past Cerberus, out at Taenarum and on to Thebes.
scenes.stakes: Laius' shade fears returning to the house of his killing.

scenes.title: Laius' phantom goads Eteocles
scenes.summary: Disguised as Tiresias, Laius tells the sleeping Eteocles that Polynices is gaining power in Argos, then shows his wound; Eteocles wakes in fury.
scenes.stakes: Eteocles risks losing his throne and life to his brother.

scenes.title: Adrastus pledges his daughters
scenes.summary: Adrastus offers his daughters to Polynices and Tydeus, who accept gladly. News spreads to Thebes.
scenes.stakes: The exiles need a home and allies.

scenes.title: Omen at Pallas' temple
scenes.summary: At the wedding procession a shield falls and a trumpet sounds in Pallas' temple, an omen of dread.
scenes.stakes: The marriage is shadowed by ill omen.

scenes.title: History of Harmonia's necklace
scenes.summary: Vulcan made the necklace for Harmonia; it brought doom to its wearers, and now Argia wears it while Eriphyle covets it.
scenes.stakes: Each owner suffers ruin; Amphiaraus and his son will be destroyed.

scenes.title: Polynices resolves to return
scenes.summary: After twelve days Polynices longs for Thebes; Argia fears for him, and Tydeus is sent as envoy.
scenes.stakes: Polynices risks exile forever or danger on his return.

scenes.title: Tydeus confronts Eteocles
scenes.summary: Tydeus travels to Thebes and demands the throne for Polynices; Eteocles refuses and Tydeus storms out with threats.
scenes.stakes: Tydeus risks his life as envoy among hostile Thebans.

scenes.title: Ambush at the Sphinx's cliff
scenes.summary: Eteocles sends fifty men to ambush Tydeus; he kills them nearly all, spares only Maeon to carry a warning.
scenes.stakes: Tydeus faces death against fifty armed men.

place.name: Cliff of the Sphinx near Thebes

scenes.title: Tydeus' trophy and prayer
scenes.summary: Tydeus hangs the spoils on an oak and vows a temple to Pallas, then returns to Argos.

Named from Mount Cyllene, his birthplace.

Tydeus' blunt demand for Polynices' promised year of rule.

analysis.text: Fraternal strife drives the book: a divine phantom and Eteocles' pride turn a broken agreement into inevitable war.
Statius uses epic conventions such as omens, ekphrasis and heroic single combat, in the Roman manner of Virgil, to frame a Greek myth.

legacy.text: The cursed necklace of Harmonia became a standard motif of fatal heirlooms in later literature.

fun_facts.text: Statius wrote the Thebaid in the late first century AD, and Dante later placed him as a Christian poet in the Purgatorio.

language_notes.text: "Winged son of Maia" is Mercury, here sent by Jove as messenger to the underworld and back.
Laius was killed by his own son Oedipus, here called his "kinsman"; the murder at a crossroads near Phocis began the curse on Thebes.
Witches of Thessaly were famed in antiquity for summoning the dead and drawing spirits from their tombs.
"Branch Lethaean" is Mercury's wand, which induces sleep, like the forgetful waters of Lethe, river of oblivion.
"Inachian folk" means the Greeks, from Inachus, legendary first king of Argos.
"Swarthy Jove" is the lord of the underworld, Pluto (Dis), called a Jove of the dead.
Arcturus is a bright star in Boötes, used here to mark the northern night sky.
Cirrha and Phocis lie near Delphi, where Laius was killed by Oedipus; his corpse polluted the land.
The yoke and bloodstained chariot recall the fatal chariot encounter in which Oedipus killed Laius.
Refers to Semele, struck by Jupiter's lightning while pregnant; Jupiter took the unborn Bacchus (Euhius) and sewed him into his thigh until birth.
Tyrian settlers: the Thebans, descended from Cadmus, who came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
Cithaeron, Rhodope and Ossa are mountains associated with Bacchic revels; the Bistonians are a Thracian people famed for frenzied worship of Bacchus.
Ogygian Iacchus: Bacchus, god of wine, called Ogygian after Ogyges, a legendary early king of Thebes.
The Cyllenian is Mercury (Hermes), born on Mount Cyllene, here sent as messenger; the Echionian prince is Eteocles, of Thebes, named for Echion.
The old man is Laius' ghost, Eteocles' grandsire, ordered to impersonate the seer Tiresias so the dream seems authoritative.
Mycenae stands for Argos and its Greeks; Cadmus is Thebes' founder. The ghost warns against Argive dominion over Thebes.
Mygdonian means Phrygian or eastern; Aurora (dawn) rises from the East. The poet uses it as a learned, decorative epithet.
'Heroes twain of Dirce and of Achelous' means Polynices (from Thebes, whose spring is Dirce) and Tydeus (from Calydon, whose river is Achelous).
'Inachian' means Argive, from Inachus, the legendary first river-god and king of Argos. It here describes Adrastus.
'Pelasgian' is a poetic term for Greek, especially Argive, peoples.
The 'sire of Pisa's bride' is Oenomaus of Pisa, who killed suitors of his daughter Hippodamia in chariot races.
Adrastus was driven from Sicyon and then took the throne of Argos, by way of his own family's earlier strife.
The 'interrupted light' refers to the sun turning away from Mycenae at the feast of Thyestes, a notorious crime of the house of Atreus.
Ogygian means Theban, from Ogyges, an ancient legendary king associated with Thebes.
'Labdacian' refers to Labdacus, grandfather of Oedipus; the 'chief' is Eteocles, ruling Thebes.
Inachus is the river-god and legendary first king of Argos; the others named are his legendary descendants, whose bronze statues fill the hall.
Phoebus' sterner sister is Diana, also called Cynthia and Delia from Mount Cynthus on Delos. Pallas is Minerva, here compared in beauty to her.
Lachesis is one of the three Fates, who assigns the length of each life's thread; her command means fate decreed this.
Munychian hills means Athens, Pallas' own city. Larissa is the citadel of Argos, where she is also worshipped.
Harmonia's necklace was a cursed heirloom of Thebes, bringing disaster to every woman who wore it. Argia's wearing it foreshadows ruin.
The Lemnian is Vulcan, worshipped on Lemnos. His wife Venus was caught in adultery with Mars; he trapped them with chains, yet the affair continued.
Telchines were legendary craftsmen-smiths, said to be early metalworkers of Rhodes, here joining the Cyclopes at Vulcan's forge.
Fruit of the Hesperides and Phrixus' fleece are the golden apples and Golden Fleece, both treasures guarded by dragons and linked to disaster.
Pasithea is one of the Graces; Charm and the Idalian youth (Cupid, from Idalium, Venus' haunt) are the kindly powers who did not make it.
Harmonia and Cadmus were turned into serpents and went to Illyria, which is the 'hissing' and furrows in the fields.
Juno, jealous of Semele's affair with Jove, came disguised and tricked her into demanding to see Jove in full glory, which killed her.
The doomed prophet is Amphiaraus, who foresees his death at Thebes; his wife Eriphyle later betrays him for this necklace.
Her son Alcmaeon later killed Eriphyle at his father's command, so his 'guiltless frenzy' alludes to matricide and madness.
"Ismenian hero" refers to Polynices through the Ismenus, a river of Thebes; "would fain" means "would gladly."
Echion was one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth; the palace is Thebes' royal house, now held by Eteocles.
Dirce is a Theban spring; "Cadmean" refers to Cadmus, Thebes' founder. Both stand for Thebes.
"Thews" means muscles or bodily strength.
"Teumesian" refers to Teumessus, a hill near Thebes, so it means Theban, here Polynices.
Juno, Argia's patron goddess, had sent her a true dream; Argia recalls it as a warning of trouble.
"The Saturnian father" is Jove, son of Saturn. "Two cities" means Argos and Thebes.
Deipyle is Argia's sister and Tydeus' wife; Tydeus is from Aetolia.
The ambassador's inviolability was a widely honored principle; Tydeus is Polynices' envoy to Eteocles, so attacking him breaks sacred custom.
The Sphinx posed a riddle to travellers near Thebes and killed those who failed; Oedipus solved it, and she threw herself from the cliff.
Olenian boar refers to Tydeus' boar-hide cloak; Olenian points to Aetolian Olenus, his homeland region. The spear's point broke off, so it did not wound him.
Pholus was a centaur who fought the Lapiths at the wedding brawl, hurling a heavy mixing-bowl. The comparison shows the boulder's size.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, opposed Bacchus and was destroyed; his descendant Phaedimus likewise meets Bacchus as a foe.
Ogygians means Thebans, after Ogyges, a legendary early king of Thebes. Bistonian means Thracian, a region linked with Mars.
Briareus was a hundred-handed giant who fought the gods in the Giants' war; Phlegra is the battlefield. Pyracmon was a Cyclops forging thunderbolts.
Euhan is a cry and title of Bacchus (Dionysus), invoked in his frenzied rites; Dryope was caught up in these revels, hence the premature birth.
Teumesian refers to Teumessus, a Theban hill; it simply means Theban. A cornel-shaft is a spear made of cornel wood.
Star-inwoven shades means the night sky, studded with stars; Menoetes swears by the night that favours Tydeus.
The triennial night is the festival of Bacchus held every third year at Thebes; Tydeus mocks the Thebans as if they were revellers, not warriors.
Tritonian maid is Pallas (Minerva), named from Lake Triton, a place linked with her birth or cult.
Guerdon means reward or recompense.
Mavors is Mars, god of war; Bellona is the Roman war goddess. Casque means helmet.
Parthaonian and Pleuron point to Tydeus' home in Aetolia; Parthaon was an ancestor of Oeneus' line. Achelous is the river there.

context_notes.text: Styx and the fiery river Phlegethon are among the rivers bounding the underworld.
Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the gates of the underworld, keeping the living out and the dead in.
Taenarum, the southern tip of the Peloponnese, was believed to hold a cave entrance to the underworld.
Neptune, god of the sea, drives horses with fish tails, according to the poet's description of the bay.
Fillets and olive branches were marks of priests and seers; Tiresias was Thebes' famous blind prophet.
Polynices married Adrastus' daughter at Argos; Tydeus, an exile for killing kin, was also welcomed there.
Laius, Eteocles' grandfather, was killed by his own son Oedipus, hence the throat wound.
Adrastus, king of Argos, had been told by an oracle to marry his daughters to a boar and a lion. He sees the two exiles as that fulfilment.
Tydeus is characteristically bold and fierce. He is an exile from Calydon, and Polynices is an exile from Thebes.
Argia and Deipyle are Adrastus's daughters. Argia will marry Polynices, and Deipyle will marry Tydeus.
Acrisius, king of Argos, was angry with Jove because the god came to his imprisoned daughter Danae as golden rain.
Brides offering their hair to a virgin goddess before marriage was a traditional rite, asking forgiveness for ending maidenhood.
Hanging captured shields in temples as trophies was customary. A falling shield and unseen trumpet were taken as bad omens.
Harmonia was the daughter of Mars and Venus, so the necklace is Vulcan's revenge on the offspring of their adultery.
Jocasta, mother and wife of Oedipus, is among the necklace's owners, whose lives ended in disaster.
Argia, daughter of Adrastus, is wife of Polynices and wears the necklace he brought from Thebes; her sister is Deipyle.
Polynices has married Argia, daughter of King Adrastus of Argos, and is staying there after being denied his share of Thebes by his brother Eteocles.
Polynices and Eteocles agreed to rule Thebes in alternate years; Eteocles' refusal to yield his throne is the cause of the war.
Tydeus had earlier fought Polynices at Adrastus' door; Adrastus took both in, recognizing a prophecy that his daughters would marry a boar and a lion.
Fortune has placed Tydeus, not Polynices, in Eteocles' power; the narrator imagines how much worse Eteocles would be toward his brother.
Dryads were tree nymphs and Fauns woodland deities; their absence shows the grove is cursed.
Chthonius is the leader of the Theban ambushers; his name suggests a link to the earth-born founders of Thebes.
Chromis is a Theban of Cadmus' line, the legendary founder of Thebes, who came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
Maeon is the one man Tydeus spares; as a seer, he foresaw the ambush's failure.
Pallas is the warrior goddess of wisdom, daughter of Jove. Her shield bears the Gorgon's head.
Diana is the virgin huntress goddess; Tydeus' father Oeneus had once neglected her, causing the Calydonian boar disaster.

literary_notes.text: Woods and fields stand amazed and Earth marvels, as if the landscape itself reacts to the unnatural journey.
The envious shade's bitter speech shows resentment surviving death, and his gloomy prediction contrasts the living world with darkness.
The peak looks down serenely and offers rest to "weary stars," making the mountain a lofty, calm being.
The ghost, sent by Jove's command, nearly flees in terror from the scene of his own murder, showing the power of his guilt-haunted memory.
The narrator's sorrowful exclamation foreshadows the doom hanging over Eteocles and Thebes while he feasts unaware.
Eteocles is compared to a negligent ship's captain idling before a storm, stressing his dangerous complacency.
The ghost's bared wound and flood of blood make the dream vivid and horrifying, spurring Eteocles' wrath.
The roused tigress seizing a man conveys Eteocles' sudden, predatory rage and the violence to come.
Dawn is a goddess who scatters shadows and shakes dew from her hair; the morning star is a rider leaving with his slow steed.
Sleep is imagined as pouring out a horn of plenty, presenting rest as a generous gift to the weary heroes.
Their relief is compared to a storm-wrecked ship sighting a friendly shore, which fits their own night of storm and exile.
Fame is a winged goddess who flies from city to city, spreading news as rumour does.
The exclamation about the monster's tongue interrupts the narration, giving the poet's disgust at Fame's hostile report.
Epithets like 'calm' Phoroneus and 'warrior' Abas, and Danaus meditating murder, give each statue a distinct character and hint at Argos' violent past.
The bride-maidens are likened to Pallas and Diana, raising them to divine beauty and stressing their virginal, awe-inspiring state.
The sudden fear and day turned to gloom signal that this marriage will bring disaster, setting up the omen to come.
The narrator addresses Argia directly, adding pathos and ominous irony as she wears the fatal necklace unknowingly.
Each ingredient, from Gorgon eyes to serpents and Tisiphone's adder, symbolizes death and ruin, making the necklace a concentrated emblem of cursed beauty.
Grief, Anguish, Discord and the Passions become the necklace's makers, showing its harm is built into it.
The narrator turns directly to Jocasta, pitying her and hinting at the horror of her marriage.
The narrator's exclamation anticipates Eriphyle's greed bringing tears and ruin, pointing to Amphiaraus' death and her own murder.
The remark that deferred hope is the heaviest burden gives a general truth about Polynices' state of mind.
The exiled bull regaining strength and returning to challenge the conqueror mirrors Polynices' brooding wrath and prepares for his return.
Argia's omens and recalled dream hint at the disaster the war will bring.
Polynices' hopeful picture of his return in royal pomp contrasts with the war and deaths that readers know await.
Fifty armed men sent against one man is compared to besieging a city, mocking the scale of the plot while honoring Tydeus.
Nature is said to have planted treachery in the place, making the landscape itself seem complicit in the crime.
Gruesome details of the Sphinx's gore, bones and talons build a horrifying picture and give the site its dark history.
The surrounding Thebans swarm like hunters driving encircled quarry into the open, making Tydeus the hunted beast.
Tydeus is likened to Briareus fending off all Olympus, elevating him to a giant's heroic scale.
One spear joins the two brothers in death, a grim image of kinship that heightens the pity of the scene.
Tydeus taunts the Thebans by contrasting their city's festivals of Bacchus with the real war they now face.
Tydeus, exhausted and gore-covered after slaughter, is compared to a gorged lion, stressing his animal ferocity and spent strength.
Tydeus' harsh command to build walls and muster troops shows his arrogance and savage pride in his own violence.
Tydeus addresses Pallas directly, praising her and piling up her haunts, in the elevated style of an epic prayer.
